fatal_errors: The proposed Mo-to-Ti substitution does not reconstruct the target intervention of adding 4.2 at.% Cr by vacuum arc melting.
It omits the decisive structural mediator: approximately 4 vol.% reticulated Cr2(Ti,Zr,Hf,Ta) Laves phase in the BCC matrix.
The claim that extra Ti will preserve high-temperature strength is unsupported and conflicts with the cited HfNbTaTiZr precedent, whose yield strength falls to 295 MPa at 1000 °C.
No evidence supports the predicted 5% density reduction or the specified strength thresholds; replacing only 20% of the Mo content would not straightforwardly imply that density change.
The experiment lacks phase-morphology, phase-fraction, lattice-parameter, fracture-strain, and hardness measurements needed to test the target mechanism.
explanation: The hypothesis recognizes the density–strength design problem and supplies numerical mechanical-property rejection criteria, so it is directionally aligned and partly falsifiable. However, it proposes a different composition change with only a generic solid-solution argument. It misses the Cr addition, lattice contraction, increased dislocation density, and reticulated Laves-phase crack-hindrance mechanism. Its outcomes also differ from the target concurrent increases in room-temperature yield strength and fracture strain—1750.6 MPa and 14.0%, respectively—and it does not test the required approximately 3.8% Laves-phase morphology. Most importantly, the preceding evidence does not justify retention of high-temperature strength after increasing Ti; it instead provides a cautionary counterexample. Thus the proposal is an inadequately supported alternative rather than a reconstruction.
